items.title: Concept: invariants, and tests that read the database
items.body:
02-CONCEPTS.md defines an **invariant**: a rule that must stay true before and after an operation. "The app works" cannot be tested. "Editing keeps the record's id" or "a failed import writes no records" can, because you can observe it.

The course's tests are built around invariants. They call the real HTTP routes and then read the PostgreSQL rows directly, rather than trusting the response alone. A status code tells you what the server *said*; reading the table tells you what it *did*.

The same chapter separates **validation** (rejecting a value the operation cannot accept) from **normalization** (turning an acceptable value into the form the program expects, such as trimming). Neither should silently invent facts.

When you read `server/test/tasks.test.cjs`, ask for each assertion: which invariant does this protect, and what wrong implementation would make it fail?

excerpts.quote: An invariant is a rule that must remain true before and after an operation.
Validation rejects values the operation cannot accept. Normalization converts acceptable values to the representation the rest of the program expects.

readMore.why: What the test suite proves, and failure experiments.

items.title: Why removing Number(row.count) turns the total into "023"
items.body:
PostgreSQL's `COUNT` returns a `bigint`. node-postgres hands bigints to JavaScript as **strings**, because JavaScript numbers cannot hold every bigint exactly. So `row.count` is "2" or "3", not 2 or 3. `stats.total` starts at the number 0. In JavaScript, `+` between a number and a string joins them as text: `0 + "2"` is "02", then `"02" + "3"` is "023". `Number(row.count)` turns each string into a real number first, so the sum is 5.

Why the others are wrong:
- Adding a string does not give NaN; `+` concatenates.
- No bigint values are involved in JavaScript here, only strings, so there is no TypeError.
- The driver does *not* convert COUNT to numbers; that is why the code calls `Number`.

excerpts.quote: for (let index = 0; index < rows.length; index += 1) { const row = rows[index]; const count = Number(row.count); stats[row.status] = count; stats.total += count; }

items.title: Why an overdue task can keep its date but not change it
items.body:
`buildUpdatePayload` handles `due_date` specially. It formats the stored date as YYYY-MM-DD (`existingDate`). If the submitted date equals it, it keeps it without running the future-date rule. Otherwise it calls `normalizeDueDate`, which requires a future date. First edit: "2020-01-01" equals the stored date, so it is accepted and the title changes: 200. Second edit: "2020-01-02" is a *changed* date, so it goes through `normalizeDueDate`, which rejects any date not in the future: 400. The test pins exactly this. The concepts chapter calls the exception "narrow".

Why the others are wrong:
- The unchanged date is exempt, so the first edit is not 400.
- The rule is not switched off for overdue tasks; changed dates are still checked.
- The title is never blocked; only a changed past date is.

excerpts.quote: if (hasOwn(payload, 'due_date')) { // An overdue task must remain editable when its existing date is submitted. const existingDate = existingTask.due_date ? toDateOnly(new Date(existingTask.due_date)) : null; updates.due_date = payload.due_date === existingDate ? existingDate : normalizeDueDate(payload.due_date); }
await api.request("PUT", `/api/tasks/${row.id}`, { due_date: "2020-01-02", }) ).status, 400,

items.title: Why resaving a done task keeps its old completed_at
items.body:
When the body contains `status`, `buildUpdatePayload` normalizes it. If the new status is "done", it sets `updates.completed_at = existingTask.completed_at || new Date()`. The `||` means: use the stored completion time if there is one, and only use "now" if there is none. The task was finished last week, so `existingTask.completed_at` has last week's timestamp, and that is what is written back. Resending every field from the form therefore does not move the completion time. Any status other than done sets `completed_at` to null.

Why the others are wrong:
- It is not reset to now; "now" is only the fallback when no time is stored.
- `completed_at` is part of the update; it is written with the reused value.
- PUT with status done sets it too; it is not toggle-only.

excerpts.quote: if (hasOwn(payload, 'status')) { updates.status = normalizeStatus(payload.status); if (updates.status === 'done') { updates.completed_at = existingTask.completed_at || new Date(); } else { updates.completed_at = null; } }

items.title: Why a status-only PUT leaves the title alone
items.body:
`buildUpdatePayload` starts with an empty `updates` object and only adds a field if the request body really has that key: `if (hasOwn(payload, 'title'))`. `hasOwn` uses `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty`, which is false for a key that was never sent. The body `{ "status": "done" }` has no title key, so `normalizeTitle` never runs and `updates.title` is never set. The SQL UPDATE only touches the columns in `updates`, so the stored title stays. The concepts chapter: "A partial update distinguishes an omitted field from a supplied null or value." (A body with `"title": null` *would* have the key and be validated.)

Why the others are wrong:
- `normalizeTitle` has no fallback to the old title; it is simply not called.
- Validation does not run for the title at all.
- The controller does not merge the body over the stored row.

excerpts.quote: function buildUpdatePayload(payload, existingTask) { const updates = {}; if (hasOwn(payload, 'title')) { updates.title = normalizeTitle(payload.title); }
function hasOwn(source, key) { return Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(source, key); }
A partial update distinguishes an omitted field from a supplied null or value.

items.title: What really rejects 2099-02-30
items.body:
"2099-02-30" has the right shape, so the regex passes. Then `new Date("2099-02-30T00:00:00.000Z")` runs. JavaScript does not make this an Invalid Date: it rolls the extra days over and gives March 2. So `getTime()` is a real number and the NaN check does not fire. The second half of that line catches it: `toDateOnly(parsed) !== value`. Formatting March 2 back gives "2099-03-02", which differs from the input, so the code throws "Due date must be a valid calendar date."

Why the others are wrong:
- The Date is valid (rolled over), not NaN.
- The service throws before any database call, so Postgres never sees it.
- 2099 is in the future, and the round-trip check runs before the future-date check anyway.

excerpts.quote: const parsed = new Date(`${value}T00:00:00.000Z`); if (Number.isNaN(parsed.getTime()) || toDateOnly(parsed) !== value) { throw new ValidationError('Due date must be a valid calendar date.'); }

items.title: Why Number.isInteger alone would accept 9007199254740992
items.body:
JavaScript numbers can represent every whole number exactly only up to 2^53 - 1 (9007199254740991). 9007199254740992 is 2^53. It is a whole number, so `Number.isInteger` says true. But it is not *safe*: nearby values like 2^53 + 1 turn into the same number, so the id may not mean what the client sent. `Number.isSafeInteger` returns false for it. `parseTaskId` uses `Number.isSafeInteger(id)` together with the range 1 to 2147483647, so the request gets 400. The concepts chapter: "Number.isInteger alone is insufficient."

Why the others are wrong:
- `Number.isInteger` has no upper limit like 2147483647; that limit is a separate check in the code.
- `Number(value)` runs first, so `isInteger` sees a number, not a string.
- `Number("9007199254740992")` is a real number, not NaN.

excerpts.quote: function parseTaskId(value) { const id = Number(value); if (!Number.isSafeInteger(id) || id < 1 || id > 2147483647) { throw new ValidationError('Task id must be a positive integer.'); }
Number.isSafeInteger rejects values JavaScript cannot represent precisely; Number.isInteger alone is insufficient.

items.title: Why the invalid-input test also counts table rows
items.body:
The test's name is the invariant: "invalid inputs are client errors and never create rows". It has two halves. The status check proves the first half: each bad POST answers 400. It cannot prove the second half. A buggy handler could insert the row and *then* throw a validation error, still answering 400 but leaving a bad record in the table. So the test counts the rows before and after, and requires the same number. Reading the real table is the only way to see what was persisted; a response code is not evidence about the database.

Why the others are wrong:
- A 422 would already fail the status assertion, which expects 400.
- The row count is about persistence, not timing.
- The test checks status codes and counts, not message wording.

excerpts.quote: test("invalid inputs are client errors and never create rows", async () => { const before = Number((await db("tasks").count("* as count").first()).count);
assert.equal( Number((await db("tasks").count("* as count").first()).count), before, );

items.title: Why a title of "<>" gets 400 "Title is required."
items.body:
`normalizeTitle` runs its steps in this order:

- `typeof value !== 'string'`? "<>" is a string, so it passes.
- `sanitizeString(value)` trims and removes every `<` and `>`. "<>" becomes "", the empty string.
- Length over 255? No.
- `title.length === 0`? Yes, so it throws "Title is required."

Because sanitizing happens *before* the empty check, a title made only of brackets counts as empty and is rejected with 400.

Why the others are wrong:
- Sanitizing does more than trim: it strips the brackets, so "<>" is not stored.
- The "must be a string" message is only for non-strings; "<>" is a string.
- The empty check runs after sanitizing, so an empty title is never stored.

excerpts.quote: function normalizeTitle(value) { if (typeof value !== 'string') { throw new ValidationError('Title is required and must be a string.'); } const title = sanitizeString(value); if (title.length > 255) throw new ValidationError('Title must be 255 characters or fewer.'); if (title.length === 0) { throw new ValidationError('Title is required.'); }
function sanitizeString(value) { return value.trim().replace(/[<>]/g, ''); }

items.title: Why the service checks title length before the database does
items.body:
The column is `table.string('title', 255)`, so Postgres would reject a 256-character title. But look at how errors become responses. `errorHandler` checks `err instanceof AppError && err.isOperational`. Only such errors keep their own status and message. A raw database error is not an AppError, so it becomes status 500 with "An unexpected error occurred." and code INTERNAL_ERROR. The client would see a server failure for what is really bad input. Checking the length in the service throws a `ValidationError` (an operational AppError), giving a useful 400. The concepts chapter: "expected bad input should produce a useful client error before a database exception."

Why the others are wrong:
- The middleware does not map database errors to 400; they become 500.
- Postgres rejects an over-long `varchar`; it does not truncate it.
- Nothing maps constraint violations to 409.

excerpts.quote: function errorHandler(err, req, res, next) { const isOperational = err instanceof AppError && err.isOperational; const statusCode = isOperational ? err.statusCode : 500; const message = isOperational ? err.message : 'An unexpected error occurred.'; const code = isOperational ? err.code : 'INTERNAL_ERROR';
if (title.length > 255) throw new ValidationError('Title must be 255 characters or fewer.');
table.string('title', 255).notNullable();

items.title: Concept: route, controller, service, model, database
items.body:
The API splits each request across layers, and each layer has one job:

- A **route** picks which handler runs for a URL.
- A **controller** turns HTTP input into arguments and the result back into a response.
- A **service** (`taskService.js`) enforces the rules: parsing ids, validating and normalizing fields, deciding what an update changes.
- A **model** (`taskModel.js`) issues the SQL through Knex.
- The **database** has the final constraints (column types, lengths).

An error middleware turns thrown errors into HTTP responses. Errors the code expects (like a validation failure) carry their own status. Anything unexpected becomes a generic server error.

So when a quiz asks "what does the client see", follow the value through every layer in order: which function sees it first, what it checks, and what kind of error it throws. A rule enforced in the service never reaches the model; a rule only the database knows reaches the client in a very different way.

excerpts.quote: Each layer has a specific responsibility. A route chooses which operation handles a URL; a controller adapts HTTP input/output; a service enforces rules; a model issues SQL.
function errorHandler(err, req, res, next) { const isOperational = err instanceof AppError && err.isOperational;

items.title: Why the search test must use % and a quote
items.body:
Concatenating the search term into SQL text means the term becomes part of the SQL. Two characters show the danger. A quote `'` ends the SQL string literal early, causing an error (or worse, injection). A percent sign `%` is a wildcard in ILIKE, so a search for "50%" would match far more rows than intended. The review for Exercise 1 asks for a **bound parameter** (`whereILike("title", ...)`), where the database treats the whole term as data, never as SQL. And it asks for a test that sends a title with `%` and `'` and "asserts the query still matches exactly the intended rows". Only such a test proves the term is bound.

Why the others are wrong:
- The guide's concern is SQL, not URL decoding.
- ILIKE can compare strings containing %; the issue is % acting as a wildcard when concatenated.
- `sanitizeString` only removes `<` and `>`, not quotes.

excerpts.quote: **Approach:** Validate a bounded search string in the service and use Knex where/whereILike binding rather than interpolating raw SQL. Test a quote and a percent sign according to the search policy.

**Review:** the filter must be a bound parameter (`whereILike("title", `%${q}%`)` or a parameterized `where`), never string-concatenated into SQL; your test sends a title containing `%` and `'` and asserts the query still matches exactly the intended rows.
function sanitizeString(value) { return value.trim().replace(/[<>]/g, ''); }

items.title: Why the second save silently overwrites the first
items.body:
`updateTask` in the service reads the task, builds the update and calls the model. The model runs `.where({ id }).update({ ...updates, updated_at: db.fn.now() })`. The only condition is the id. Nothing says "only if nobody changed it since I loaded it", and the table has no version column. So both PUTs match, both succeed with 200, and the second simply writes over the first: **last write wins**. Exercise 3 is exactly about fixing this: add a `version` column, update `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?`, and answer 409 when no row matches.

Why the others are wrong:
- The database does not merge; each UPDATE replaces the columns it sets.
- The UPDATEs do not block each other into a failure; both succeed.
- `updated_at` is only written, never compared, so nothing returns 409 today.

excerpts.quote: async function updateTask(id, updates) { const rows = await tasksTable() .where({ id }) .update({ ...updates, updated_at: db.fn.now() }) .returning('*');
add a `version` column, send it back on `PUT`, update with `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` and answer 409 on zero rows

items.title: Start here: the Task Manager API course and its reading order
items.body:
This pack uses `01-task-manager` in the newcodexjs repo: an Express API with a PostgreSQL database (through Knex) and a React client for a simple task list. The course in `01-task-manager/astraupskill/` treats one small validation change as a complete CRUD boundary.

Read in this order:

- **astraupskill/README.md**: what you will be able to do, prerequisites, and how to start the project and its separate test database.
- **01-CODEBASE-MAP.md**: which file handles which step of a request.
- **02-CONCEPTS.md**: layers, invariants, validation versus normalization, state transitions and identity.
- **03-WORKED-CHANGE.md**, then **04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md**: the change and how its tests prove it.
- **05-PRACTICE.md**, then **06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md**: exercises first, then solution guidance and review questions.

Most quizzes ask what one function does with a specific input. Keep `server/src/services/taskService.js` and `server/src/models/taskModel.js` open and trace the input line by line.

excerpts.quote: The central skill is **HTTP contracts, service validation and real SQL persistence**.
- Trace an action from input through validation, state/persistence and output. - Predict a success case and a failure case before running either.

items.title: What keeps a malicious order value out of orderByRaw
items.body:
`orderByRaw` inserts its string into SQL as it is: `${filters.order}` is pasted in, not bound. So the model is only safe if `filters.order` can never hold anything dangerous. That guarantee comes from the service. `normalizeListFilters` sets `filters.order = validateAllowedValue('order', ..., VALID_ORDERS)`, an **allowlist** of asc and desc. "asc;DROP TABLE tasks" is not on the list, so the service throws a validation error (400) before the model ever runs. The raw SQL is safe only because of that earlier layer.

Why the others are wrong:
- `orderByRaw` does not escape or bind interpolated text; that is what "raw" means.
- Express has no rule against semicolons in query strings.
- The guide does not rely on Postgres refusing multiple statements; the allowlist is the protection.

excerpts.quote: if (filters.sort === 'priority') { query.orderByRaw(`CASE priority WHEN 'low' THEN 1 WHEN 'medium' THEN 2 WHEN 'high' THEN 3 END ${filters.order}`); } else if (filters.sort === 'due_date') { query.orderByRaw(`due_date ${filters.order} NULLS LAST`);
if (query.order) { filters.order = validateAllowedValue('order', String(query.order).toLowerCase(), VALID_ORDERS); }
